title: Basic geometrical ideas and elementary shapes
subject: Mathematics
summary: Geometry begins with points, lines, line segments, rays and angles, and with measuring and classifying shapes.
points: A point has position, a line extends in both directions, a ray has one end and a line segment has two.
Angles are acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex, and are measured in degrees with a protractor.
Triangles are classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles.
Quadrilaterals include squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombuses and trapeziums.
A circle has a centre, radius, diameter, chord and arc.
example: An angle of 120° is obtuse because it is more than 90° and less than 180°.
mistakes: Confusing a line with a line segment.
Measuring an angle from the wrong zero mark on the protractor.

title: Areas related to circles
subject: Mathematics
summary: The area and perimeter of circles extend to sectors, segments and combinations of plane figures.
points: Circumference is 2πr and area is πr².
A sector is a pie-shaped part bounded by two radii and an arc.
A segment is the region between a chord and the corresponding arc.
Problems often combine circles with squares, triangles or semicircles; add or subtract areas carefully.
example: A 90° sector of a circle of radius 7 cm has area ¼ × 22/7 × 49 = 38.5 cm².
mistakes: Using the diameter as the radius.
Forgetting to subtract the triangle when finding a segment.

title: Conservation of plants and animals
subject: Science
summary: Deforestation and habitat loss threaten species, and conservation protects wildlife, forests and ecosystems.
points: Deforestation causes soil erosion, flooding, desertification and loss of species.
Endangered species face extinction; endemic species live only in one region.
National parks, sanctuaries and biosphere reserves protect habitats in place.
Zoos, seed banks and breeding programmes conserve species outside their habitat.
Reforestation and community forest management restore degraded land.
example: Project Tiger protects tiger habitats and also conserves the species that share them.
mistakes: Thinking conservation means only protecting animals.
Ignoring habitat loss as the main threat.

title: The making of a global world
subject: History
summary: Trade, migration, colonialism and technology wove distant regions into a single world economy over five centuries.
points: The silk routes linked Asia, Africa and Europe long before modern globalisation.
Columbus's voyages connected the Americas to Eurasia and began the Columbian exchange.
The slave trade and indentured labour moved millions of people across oceans.
The nineteenth century saw free trade, railways and steamships integrate markets.
The Great Depression of the 1930s showed how connected economies had become.
example: Potatoes, maize and chillies reached India from the Americas through global exchange.
mistakes: Ignoring forced migration in global trade.

title: Era of one-party dominance
subject: Political Science
summary: From 1952 to 1967 the Congress won national elections repeatedly, shaping India's early democratic practice.
points: The Congress drew on the freedom movement's prestige and a broad coalition of social groups.
Opposition parties were fragmented and often lacked national reach.
Internal factionalism within the Congress acted as a channel for dissent.
The party's dominance was electoral, not the only legal party, so elections remained competitive.
This era ended with coalition politics and the rise of regional parties.
example: The 1952, 1957 and 1962 general elections gave the Congress large majorities in the Lok Sabha.

title: Regional aspirations
subject: Political Science
summary: Regional movements in Punjab, Assam, the North-East and Jammu and Kashmir tested India's federal accommodation.
points: The Punjab crisis involved demands for greater autonomy and led to the Anandpur Sahib resolution and later accord.
The Assam movement opposed illegal migration and produced the Assam Accord of 1985.
North-Eastern states demanded autonomy and statehood, met through reorganisation and special provisions.
Jammu and Kashmir's special status under Article 370 was altered in 2019.
Accommodation through negotiation has been more successful than suppression.
example: The Assam Accord set a cut-off date for identifying foreign nationals in Assam.
mistakes: Treating all regional demands as separatist.

title: Principles of management
subject: Business Studies
summary: Management principles are general guidelines; Fayol's fourteen principles and Taylor's scientific management are the classic frameworks.
points: Fayol's principles include division of work, authority and responsibility, unity of command, unity of direction, and scalar chain.
Other Fayol principles include discipline, subordination of individual interest, remuneration, centralisation and esprit de corps.
Taylor's scientific management used time study, motion study and standardisation.
Taylor separated planning from execution and introduced functional foremanship.
Principles are guidelines, not rigid rules, and must suit the situation.

formulas.name: Taylor's technique
formulas.expr: standard output per worker per day = optimum time from time and motion study

example: Unity of command means an employee should receive orders from only one superior.
mistakes: Treating principles as laws with guaranteed results.
Confusing unity of command with unity of direction.
